An interesting idea. I usually don't go for these sorts of ideas but so long as it was a true lottery, I wouldn't have a tremendous objection to it.
Random selections aren't based on merit. And there's a risk of them saying it's random, but then rigging the results to favor whoever they want.

So I'm with you on rigging, but I would contend that the system isn't as meritorious as you might think. My line of reasoning is simply this, middle class America is severely under represented at the Ivies. As a middle class (public school) kid you better have parents who went to that institution. This type of lottery isn't going to benefit who the author thinks it will. It would benefit the middle class. The kinds of kids who don't have money privilege or POC privilege.

An anecdote (yes I realize anecdotes are week sauce but it's what I have to work with)
So two kids from my high school applied to Harvard (IIRC) one was our valedictorian all everything. The other was an extremely smart young lady who didn't quite have the same grades or SAT scores but one of her parents went to Harvard. They didn't take the valedictorian but took the less qualified young lady (I don't think gender played much of a role here but is quasi pertinent). The two of them had the same extracurriculars (they were dating and did everything together). In any meritorious system the valedictorian would have been taken over his less qualified gf.

The Ivies routinely look at factors beyond merit to make these types of decisions. IMO is hard to impossible to compare kids who all basically have the same credentials. American high schools just aren't good at discriminating between students in the top five percent or so. They all have similar GPAs, community involvement, and good SAT scores. Particularly with GPAs and SAT scores these factors have intentionally been leveled at the top end to minimize differences between a 98% and a 99.9% kid. This allows a much larger pool for these institutions to choose from on factors outside of merit (ability to pay, legacy status, ethnicity, etc). In 1995 they denormed the SAT to separate it from IQ (before that it was a relatively strong indicator of IQ). This essentially hurt middle class kids. A strong SAT score (correlated to a high IQ) was their strongest bargaining factor for admission into one of these institutions. Now universities have a large undifferentiated mass of kids who could all by "merit" reasonably achieve admission into one of these institutions. I don't have an issue with a merit based system but by and large that has been intentionally made impossible.

They always give unfair preferential treatment if you have family members who went there before. But they are also extremely expensive in terms of tuition and other costs, so much so that some middle class students can't compete with other rich private school kids, despite equaling or exceeding their achievements.
